nameStory: This millipede has a recently proposed common name of 'Bob's Yellow and Black Millipede,' though the story behind who 'Bob' is remains a mystery in the scientific literature. The scientific name 'trimaculata' means 'three-spotted,' referring to the distinctive markings that help identify this species. Sometimes the most straightforward names are the most useful for field identification!
description: Bob's Yellow and Black Millipede is a small, cylindrical millipede that belongs to the cherry millipede family. Like all millipedes, it has two pairs of legs per body segment and curls into a tight coil when disturbed. This species displays the characteristic yellow and black coloration that gives it its common name. It's one of the smaller millipedes you'll encounter in New England forests.

idTips.label: Yellow and black pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinctive yellow and black striping or banding along the body segments - this coloration pattern is your best field mark and stands out against dark forest floor debris

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Small and cylindrical with a smooth, somewhat shiny appearance when you examine it closely - feels firm but not hard when gently handled

idTips.label: Coiling behavior
idTips.description: Curls into a tight spiral when touched or disturbed, like a tiny watch spring - this defensive posture is typical of millipedes but watch for the yellow-black pattern even when coiled

idTips.label: Movement pattern
idTips.description: Moves slowly with a wave-like motion of its many legs, quite different from the quick darting of centipedes - you can easily keep pace with it as it crawls

idTips.label: Three-spotted marking
idTips.description: The 'trimaculata' name refers to three-spotted markings, though these may require close examination with a hand lens to see clearly

habitat: Look for this millipede in moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially under rotting logs, leaf litter, and decomposing organic matter. They prefer areas with rich, damp soil where they can feed on decaying plant material. You're most likely to find them by gently turning over fallen logs or raking through the leaf litter in mature forest settings.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms up, often found under logs and in leaf litter as they emerge from winter hiding spots. Good time to search as vegetation is still sparse.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're easiest to find foraging in moist areas. Look during cooler parts of the day or after rain when they venture closer to the surface.
seasonality.fall: Still active as they prepare for winter, often concentrating under logs and in deep leaf litter. The fresh fallen leaves provide both food and shelter.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in soil, under logs, or in protected crevices. Rarely seen unless you dig deep into leaf litter on warmer winter days.

funFact: Despite being called 'millipede' (meaning 'thousand feet'), no millipede actually has 1,000 legs - most have between 30 and 400 legs, and this species is on the lower end of that range, but it can still coordinate all those legs to move in perfect wave-like synchronization!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, dark millipedes in the leaf litter, but the yellow and black coloration is distinctive among New England millipedes. Remember: millipedes coil up and move slowly, while centipedes (which can also be striped) run quickly and don't coil - think 'mellow millipede' versus 'crazy centipede.'
contextualKnowledge: The recent proposal of 'Bob's Yellow and Black Millipede' as a common name reflects ongoing efforts to give user-friendly names to invertebrates that previously only had scientific names. Many millipedes are still known primarily by their Latin names, making field identification more challenging for citizen scientists.
compareHints: This appears to be the only Rudiloria species in New England, making it unique in its genus regionally. Compared to other cherry millipedes (family Xystodesmidae), Bob's Yellow and Black Millipede is distinguished by its specific yellow and black patterning rather than the cherry-red colors typical of other family members. The three-spotted feature referenced in its scientific name also sets it apart from relatives.
